items.title: 21.1.2 Defence Provided by Digestive and Respiratory Tracts

blocks.text: Many bacteria are present in the food that humans eat. Most of these are killed by saliva in the oral cavity, which also contains lysozyme. The strong digestive acids present in the stomach and the protein-digesting enzymes in the intestine also kill bacteria.

Many microbes are present in the air that we breathe. Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria before they can enter the air passageway. The cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles secrete a layer of sticky mucous that traps microbes before they can reach the warm, moist lungs. Cilia on the cells lining these passages continually sweep the mucous upward, where it can be swallowed.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book uses “mucous” as a noun (“sticky mucous”, “the mucous upward”). Mucous is the adjective (as in mucous cells); the sticky secretion is mucus.

blocks.alt: A strip of tracheal epithelium: columnar cells with mucous cells among them, cilia on their free surface, and a mucous layer over the cilia with trapped microbes in it. An upward arrow shows the movement of mucus. A small inset shows the head, trachea and lungs, with a box on the trachea.
